doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: How to play the thump and rhythm guitar
summary: Technique of bottom-string triads in rhythm guitar, why young players should play rhythm, and Pallo's preference for trios without drums.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Is it a four thumps per measure or is it more of a two and four?

It’s according to if you’re doing it on a two and then to a four. Exactly. Right. But I would say on a ballad you would hear it more on the two and four. And so listen to it with Johnny Mathis way back and you’ll hear Tony Mottola in the background on that.
Like “Chances Are?” That kind of tune?
Yes. “Chances Are,” every one he did, “Misty,” all his first records he ever did. And then Bucky does the same thing now if you notice.
How do you thump? I mean what is it that —

Well first of all you don’t use all six strings, you try to stay with the bottom strings, and you have to make sure, like even Bucky says it to me that you don’t have to play — if a thirteenth comes up on your music you don’t have to play the thirteenth, just play the © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

triad or whatever it is, and just make sure you do it, and it would be like in elevenths and more like that, and you don’t even have to — if the trumpets are playing the thirteenths and all that it doesn’t affect you at all because you’re just playing the basic, the root, the fifth — make sure you get that in there.

That’s something that really needs to be told to young guitar players like in big bands, because I see these high school kids and they see the music and I see them trying to get all this stuff. And there no way — and not only can’t they do it but they shouldn’t because it doesn’t sound right.

No. No you don’t have to because then you have the horn section doing that or the string section doing that, so, if you’re going to play rhythm, if you are going to play rhythm. But how many are playing rhythm today though. That’s, every guitar player, young guitar players want to get out there and play that lead and there are a few though, being with Les Paul I say three people a night, every Monday night, being with Les 23 years now, come up and say, “Gee I’d love to play rhythm guitar.” And when you hear it from a youngster it makes me feel so good. It’s not that — I love rock & roll too. I love all kinds of music. There’s good and bad. But when they talk about rhythm that’s real rhythm. It’s the real stuff, back then.
You could almost have a band without a drummer when you have that thing going like that.

Exactly. That’s why if I do a special job and I need a trio I’d rather use a bass player and no drums at all, maybe keyboard, bass and myself or a trumpet, bass and myself or whatever. And I’ll be the drummer.
You should get paid twice you know that.
That’d be — you know you’re right. I should get double fee. That’s true.
